text.front:
Hiding the machine: stories, rights and the
naturalisation of corporate technology
Eduardo Gill-Pedro
Associate Senior Lecturer, Faculty of Law, Lund University, Lund, Sweden
ABSTRACT
This article shows how two powerful narratives, or 'stories', about corporations
were developed and refined by different groups of scholars over specific
periods of time as a response to growing concerns about the size and power
of corporations, concerns which motivated calls for greater regulation. The
stories responded to these concerns by an impressive feat of prestidigitation:
each of these stories made the company disappear. The article argues
that these 'stories' about corporations work in tandem with corresponding
stories about the rights of such corporations. The former work as shields,
which can be deployed in a range of policy spaces to counter calls for
greater control over the power of corporations. The latter work as swords-
the rights stories allow corporations to challenge restrictions on the exercise
of their power, without foregrounding the corporation as the subject of
those rights.
ARTICLE HISTORY Received 15 July 2024; Accepted 21 February 2025
KEYWORDS Rights of corporations; theory of the firm; nexus of contracts; entrepreneur; narratives
text.body:
1. Introduction
Companies-for-profit commercial corporations-have played a central
role in shaping our current political, legal, economic and social orders.
Their superhuman capabilities and the enormous resources at their disposal
has allowed them to massively transform our natural and social environ-
ment. Some argue that we are not living in the Anthropocene, but rather
in the Technocene-a geological era brought about not by the psycho-phys-
iological make up of human beings, but by technological agency. 1 The

modern company, a form of legal technology, is the central element of this
agency.
And yet, in legal theory and practice, the company has had remarkably
low visibility. Companies are either subsumed under the broader category
of 'personhood' and treated as indistinguishable from other kinds of legal
persons, or they are regarded as mere fictions, labels that facilitate inter-
actions between human persons. Methodological individualism has pre-
vailed, with the focus on individual human beings and their relationship
with each other, with the state or other public entities, rather than on
private corporate entities.
The aim of this article is to show that this low visibility of the company is the
outcome of two specific narratives, or 'stories', about companies that have been
constructed over the past century. The first story can be called 'the nexus of con-
tracts' story, the second, 'the entrepreneur' story. I will show how each of these
stories was developed and refined by different groups of scholars over specific
periods of time and how each of these stories responded to growing concerns
about the size and power of companies, concerns which motivated calls for
greater regulation and democratic control over companies. These stories
responded to these concerns by an impressive feat of prestidigitation: each of
these stories made the company disappear. The focus shifted from the corpor-
ation, as a contingent and artificial technology, to the human beings within and
behind the corporation, human beings who interact in ways that are presented
as necessary and natural.
I will then examine the caselaw of the United States (US) Supreme Court
and show how its caselaw on the rights of companies might fit and justify the
'nexus of contract' story, and the caselaw of the Court of Justice of the Euro-
pean Union (EU), and how its caselaw on the right to conduct business
might fit and justify the 'entrepreneur' story. I will argue that these stories
work in tandem. The stories about companies work as shields, which can
be deployed in a range of policy spaces to counter calls for greater control
over the power of corporations, by presenting regulation of the market by
the state as interference in spontaneous processes, driven by individuals, pro-
cesses which, if left alone, result in better societal outcomes. The stories
about rights work as swords, by allowing corporations to challenge restric-
tions on the exercise of their power, without foregrounding the corporation
as the subject of those rights.
I conclude by arguing that, taken together, these narratives hinder our
ability to perceive and engage with corporate power as power that is
vested in, and yielded by, the corporations themselves.
Before telling these stories, I will lay the ground by arguing that corpor-
ations are a form of legal technology that was constructed as a result of
specific political decisions, and that this technology has been the subject of
controversy and contestation from the beginning.

2. The corporation as a contested technology
Business corporations occupy such a ubiquitous place in our modern
societies that it is easy to regard them as natural and inevitable phenomena.
In this section I will seek to present corporations as a specific kind of tech-
nology that was created to achieve human ends. I will show that, contrary to
what is claimed by the 'nexus of contracts' and 'entrepreneur' stories,
business corporations did not arise naturally out of voluntary transactions
between individuals in the market, nor did they arise spontaneously as an
inevitable element of a market. Instead, business corporations are best
understood as a contingent and constructed technology I will demonstrate
the contingent and constructed nature of the modern business corporation
by showing that that the components that make up corporate technology
developed over hundreds of years, and have only come together in the
modern business corporation fairly recently, in the course of the nineteenth
century. I will further show that the development of the business corporation
has been controversial from the start, and that concerns about the impact of
this technology on human society have persisted.
I am aware that engaging with this topic entails engaging with the vexed
topic of the nature of the corporate legal person. 2 In using the metaphor of
'technology' rather than 'person', I seek to avoid anthropomorphism associ-
ated with the word 'person' and to keep the focus on the business corpor-
ation as a legal construct. 3 I build on Dan-Cohen's metaphor of the
business corporation as an intelligent machine 4 , and this approach chimes
with Bruner's conceptualisation of the corporation as 'technology'. 5 It does
not entail any commitment to an understanding of the corporation as a
real entity in the sense of a social phenomenon that has an existence
outside of, and prior to, the law. 6
2.1. The components of the technology
While the technology of the business corporation is 'remarkably adaptive'
and exists in different forms in different societies and political systems, 7
there are a few key components that underpin its status as 'undoubtably

one of the most important societal devices that human beings have ever
invented'. 8 Abatino et al 9 list four components of the modern corporate
form that underpin its success: Continuity, direct agency, limited liability
and entity shielding. These features turn a business association into an entity.
2.1.1. Continuity
Continuity refers to the ability of business corporations to persist despite the
death or withdrawal of any investor, director or employee of the corporation.
Modern corporations are, as Lynn Stout puts it, 'sempiternal': once created
they can, in principle, last forever. 10 This continuity frees the corporation
from dependency on any particular individual or groups. It also, as Stout
points out, allows present generations to commit capital to 'long-term pro-
jects whose benefits will not be realized until well after the current cohort of
human beings has ceased to exist'. 11
Continuity in business entities is a fairly recent phenomenon. Roman
business associations lacked any form of continuity. The Societas was a
form of partnership whereby a group of citizens embarked on a common
enterprise and agreed to share the profits. 12 This partnership enjoyed no con-
tinuity, and 'existed only for as long as all (and only) the original partners
participated'. 13
In Medieval Europe, corporations were created to make possible 'long-
term projects whose benefits will not be realized until well after the
current cohort of human beings has ceased to exist', such as the construction
of cathedrals and universities. 14 Such goals required the creation of legal
form endowed with separate legal personality and perpetual life, through
which present generations would be able to commit assets to be used to
achieve goals that would be realised by future generations. However, such
entities required a Royal or Papal charter, and were deployed for religious
or public ends. There were some business associations that arose in Medieval
Italy enjoyed greater continuity, but were still connected to, and dependent
on, wealthy individuals or families. 15

The Joint Stock Companies that arose in the Low Countries and in
England in the Sixteenth Century, most famously the Duch East India
Company (VOC) chartered to exploit trade in the Asia, were originally liqui-
dated at the end of each voyage. It required legislation by the Dutch Estates
General to grant the VOC perpetual existence. 16 In England, the East India
Company was granted a Royal Charter in 1600, but originally only for 15
years. The Charter was successively renewed until its dissolution, but the
English (and British) parliament were reluctant to grant further charters
and the renewal of the East India Company's charter became increasingly
contested. 17 It was only with the incorporation acts of the mid-nineteenth
century that business associations with continuity of existence became
readily available.
2.1.2. Direct agency
In order for the corporation to be able to operate in the market, by
buying and selling property, entering into contracts, enforcing their rights
in court, and so on, it needs direct agency, that is, the ability to delegate
to specific natural persons the authority to act in the name of the
corporation. 18
According to Fleckner, Roman law did not developed a general
agency regime. 19 While the partners of a societas were able to hire an
institor for the day-to-day management of the business 20 , the institor acted
on behalf of the natural person who employed him, not on behalf of the
societas.
The early English corporations were chartered with the requirement to
have a board of directors that acted collectively and on behalf of the
company, rather than as representatives of the individual the shareholders. 21
Even 'deed of settlement' joint stock companies would typically include a
clause that allocated the authority to manage the company on a board of
directors, rather than on the stockholders. Finaly, with the enactment of
general incorporation statutes in England, a provision that the directors

By having decision making authority assigned to specific individuals
appointed collectively, the power of any individual shareholder is reduced,
and the company is able to function more effectively as an entity.
2.1.3. Entity shielding
Entity shielding vests the assets of the firm in the firm itself and protects
those assets from either the personal creditors of the 'owners' 23 in the firm
-weak entity shielding-or also from the investors themselves-strong
entity shielding, that includes some kind of investment lock-in-which pre-
vents the investors from forcing the liquidation of his investment. Hans-
mann, Kraakman and Squire insist that entity shielding is the sine qua non
of legal entities. 24
There is reasonable agreement that there were no commercial entities that
benefited from entity shielding in Roman times. 25 The solvency and there-
fore the viability (as a going concern) of societas was dependent on the sol-
vency of the partners. In addition, as Dari-Matiacci et al note, 'Roman law
adhered strictly to the principle of exit at will', 26 which meant that any
attempt to provide strong entity shielding, by locking in the investment
and preventing forced liquidation of the investment would not be enforce-
able in court.
This was to change with the advent, in medieval Italy, of a compagnias that
enjoyed what Hansmann et al describe as 'a weak form of entity shielding'.
Under this regime, the compagnia's creditors enjoyed a claim to the compag-
nia's assets 'that was prior to the claim of the partner's personal creditors'. 27

legal and ideological implications that are not accepted in this article, but in order to be faithful to the
literature the term owner will be used, but in quotes.

The claim rather is that the advent of entity shielding is of greater importance 'for the creation of

But it was in Low Countries in early 1600 that strong entity shielding
emerged. The Charter of the Dutch East India Company provided perma-
nent capital lock-in, 28 which not only shielded the VOC from the claims
by the investors' creditors, but also included liquidation protection; no inves-
tor could unilaterally liquidate the company in order to force the payout of
that investor's share. 29
Entity shielding is a key component in the emergence of the legal technol-
ogy that has become the modern company. There are three key elements to
its relevance in this article.
First, entity shielding emancipates the legal entity from its owners. It
enables the firm to exist and to trade in its own name. The assets of the
firm belong to the firm and are not at the disposal of the investors. The via-
bility of the firm as a going concern is not dependent on the financial viability
of any individual investors. Entity shielding allows the firm creditworthiness
to be based solely on the firm itself. If there is no entity shielding, a trader
that considers entering into a contract with a firm will need to assess the
financial soundness not only of the firm but also of all the owners of the
firm. If an owner's creditors can draw on the firm's assets to repay the
owner's debts, then there may not be sufficient assets in the firm to also
pay the firm's creditors. With entity shielding, anyone considering contract-
ing with the firm will only need to assess the financial soundness of the firm
itself.
Second, entity shielding requires special rules of property law 30 that create
these shielded legal entities. It requires the development of a new kind of
legal technology to do something that cannot be achieved by contractual
arrangements. 31
Third, entity shielding depends on other technological developments.
Hansmann et al describe how the invention of double entry book-keeping,
the adoption of Arabic rather than Roman numerals, and the evolution of
paper making technology made it possible for firms to keep consistent and
accurate records of their assets and liabilities. 32 This again emancipated
the firm from its human investors, as it allowed creditors 'to accept a
firm's business assets, rather than the personal assets of its owners, or the
text.note:
31 It could, in theory, be possible for a group of investors to enter into a contract where they will agree
not to force the liquidation of the firm, nor to withdraw their capital unless the majority of investors
agree. But they would also need to ensure that every other contract that those investors make will
include a clause that will prevent any claim on the investors from attaching to that investor's
assets held in the firm. Not only would such a requirement be impossible for the other investors
to monitor, but it would also be unlikely that such a clause would be enforced by a court, as it
would entail imposing obligations on third parties not privy to the contract.

trustworthiness of any particular owner or agent, as the principal bond for
the firm's obligations'. 33
2.1.4. Limited liability
Limited Liability can be described as the flip side of entity shielding. Both are
necessary components in what Margaret Blair calls asset partitioning, 34 that
is to say, the separation of the assets of the corporation from the share-
holders. Whereas entity shielding protects the corporation's assets from
the investor's creditors and from the investors themselves, limited liability
(or owner shielding, as Hansmann et al 35 put it) protects the investors
from liabilities incurred by the corporation.
Whilst limited liability has been described as a 'an essential precondition
for the development of widely held corporations, stock markets and indus-
trial economies', 36 Harris shows that it has only become widespread in its
usage in the twentieth century.
There is evidence that, in Ancient Rome, there was a legal form that
enjoyed a degree of limited liability. The peculium was a 'common practice
[whereby] a master provide[d] his slave … with a set of assets, termed a pecu-
lium, for use in a business venture' 37 If the master did not participate in the
management of the peculium, he would be shielded from any liability for
amounts that exceeded the value of the peculium. 38 However, the peculium
did not enjoy any kind of entity shielding, nor could it be termed a business
association, in the true sense of the word. 39
Harris describes how the development of limited liability in the modern
period can be divided into three periods. Period I, from 1600 to 1800,
when early corporations such as the Dutch and English (then British) East
India Company were able to grow into giants with thousands of shareholders
raising millions of guilders and pounds of capital, all without providing
limited liability to those shareholders. 40 Period II, from 1800 the early
1900s saw the introduction of the general incorporation acts in the UK

ing' (2020) 16 Journal of Institutional Economics 643, at 643.

39 According to Fleckner the sources do not support the assumption that the peculium of common slaves
was used to fund larger enterprises. Fleckner (n 19).

rule as we understand it today. 41 Rather, it allowed the promoters of the
company to draft into the Articles of Association the extent of liability
that members would be subject to, and in fact, during this period '[limited
liability] was only adopted by a small number of business corporations'. 42
It was only in Period III, from 1900 to the present day, that the choice of
limited liability became the norm for incorporating companies.
2.2. The corporate entity
As Margaret Blair points out, it is the nature of the corporation as an entity
that distinguishes it 'from other collaborative approaches to carrying out
business activities, such as partnerships, or alliances, or just ordinary con-
tracts'. 43 The claim advanced in this article is that this entity is a form of
legal technology constructed from these four components of continuity,
direct agency, entity shielding and limited liability. 44
2.3. The company as a contested political project
In the previous section I highlighted the contingent nature of corporate tech-
nology, 45 and of how the different components of that technology were
developed over time. Companies did not arise naturally, as a result of spon-
taneous interactions between individuals, or as the inevitable outcome of
social and technological change. Rather, 'The company needs to be under-
stood as an institution which had in part to be deliberately constructed
through political and legal agency'. 46 In this section I argue that the develop-
ment of the technology of the corporation was, from the very start, a con-
tested project, and has remained so to this day.
Adam Smith, who is often identified as the father of modern capitalism,
was highly critical of joint stock companies. This criticism has often been
portrayed as mistaken pessimism about the economic efficiency of corpor-
ations, 47 or as being a response to the monopolistic nature of the contem-
poraneous companies, 48 However, as Muthu points out, Smith's critique is

because the 'fraud and abuse inseparable from the management of the
affairs of so great a company'. 50 Furthermore, the power that accrues to
such corporations causes them to act as sovereign over vast swathes of
people about whom the corporations agents care or know little. 51 While
the sovereign is supposed to embody the interests of the people they
govern, merchants who act as sovereigns have the opposite interest. 52
Smith also feared that the extraordinary concentration of economic power
at the hands of such corporations would enable them to distort domestic pol-
itical processes to their advantage. 53 While Fleckner claims that 'it is difficult
to find an area where Smith was as wrong as in his gloomy forecast of the
joint stock company', 54 one could argue that he was instead highly prophetic
in identifying, at such an early stage, the concerns with corporate power that
animate political economists to this day. 55
Smith was not alone in his objections to the emergence of business cor-
porations. As William Roy notes, on the other side of the Atlantic there
were strong republican objections to the privileges enjoyed by corporations,
and to the power that they accrued, at the expense of the people or of the
state. 56 One of the founding fathers, Thomas Jefferson, famously hoped to
be able to 'crush … the aristocracy of our monied corporations which dare
already to challenge our government to a trial of strength and bid defiance
to the laws of our country'. 57
These objections were overcome, and the general incorporation statutes of
the mid nineteenth century led to a great increase in the number, size and
power of business corporations.
This growth in the number and scale of incorporations led to renewed
concern about corporate power in the early part of the twentieth century.
Berle and Means argue that the modern company, 'involves a concentration
of power in the economic field comparable to the concentration of religious

This concentration of power gives rise to the 'insistence that power in
[modern corporations] shall be subjected to the same tests of public
benefit which have been applied in their turn to power [held by Churches
and by States]'. 59 Modern companies should not be analysed as private
organisations but should instead be considered social entities. Their
purpose should therefore be to serve, 'not alone the owners or the control
but all society'. 60 In the first half of the twentieth century, the business cor-
poration became increasingly seen as 'an economic institution which has a
social service as well as a profit-making function'. 61
The 1960s and 70s saw a fierce debate arise, especially in the United
States, about the growth of the scope and power of corporations, and the
social and environmental harm that they caused. As Grindis notes, Ralph
Nader's high profile campaign 'was behind the adoption of a series of con-
sumer, worker, and environmental protection regulations in the late
1960s' 62 as well as to the creation of Federal regulatory agencies, able to
regulate and constrain corporate activity. Even business leaders accepted
that corporations must be governed so as to operate in a socially respon-
sible way. In 1971, the Committee for Economic Development, a
business-led think-tank, published a statement on 'The Social Responsibil-
ities of Business Corporations' acknowledging that 'the corporation is
regarded and operated as a permanent institution in society' 63 and that
its manager must therefore act to 'serve constructively the needs of
society'. 64
The next two sections will present two stories about the company which
can be seen as a response to these calls for greater control and oversight. The
claim in this paper is not that the development of these stories has been some
kind of conspiracy by nefarious actors. Rather, in the spirit of Chan and
Hansen's arguments, the claim is that these stories have emerged as 'legiti-
mating schema' which reflect and support the 'situational power' of corpor-
ate interests, 65 and which have the effect of deflecting concerns about that
power.

3. The nexus of contracts story
The calls to impose greater responsibilities on companies were famously
challenged by Milton Friedman. Friedman denied that corporations could
have responsibilities-talk of corporate responsibility referred to the respon-
sibility of individual corporate executives who argued that:
a corporate executive is an employee of the owners of the business. He has
direct responsibility to his employers. That responsibility is to conduct the
business in accordance with their desires, which generally will be to make as
much money as possible. 66
To ask a corporate executive to spend the corporation's money on pursuing
social goals, is both wrong in principle and in outcome. On the one hand, the
executive is effectively taxing the stockholders from profits that they would
otherwise receive, even though he [sic] has no legitimacy to make those
kinds of decisions, as he is not elected according to the proper political pro-
cesses. On the other he has no expertise on how social goals should be best
achieved.
According to Friedman, the responsibility of business was 'to use its
resources and engage in activities designed to increase its profits'. 67 So
while Friedman denied the concept of corporate (social) responsibility
(CSR), the way he framed the 'responsibility of business' still pits one under-
standing of the objective of the corporation directly against the CSR
approach. In other words, he argued that the objective of the corporation
should be the pursuit of profit for its shareholders, rather than the broader
range of objectives advocated by CSR proponents.
Politically, the argument that corporations should not have socially ben-
eficial objectives but should instead have as their objective solely the enrich-
ment of its shareholders, was a hard sell. Michael Jensen and William
Meckling were sympathetic to the argument, but were convinced that his
arguments needed to be 'translated "into the language of economics"'. 68
Their famous article on the theory of the firm 69 supported Friedman's argu-
ment that the manager of a firm is an agent of the stockholders. 70 However,
they go on to argue that the firm is a 'legal fiction […] which serve[s] as a
nexus for a set of contractual obligations among individuals'. 71 Viewing
firms in this way means that questions about the objective function of the
firm, and arguments about whether firms should have social responsibility

Magazine (13 September 1970).

69 Michael Jensen and William Meckling, 'Theory of the Firm: Managerial Behavior, Agency Costs and

was nonsensical. Firms are not like individuals and can have no motivations
or intentions. The 'behaviour' of firms was 'like the behaviour of the
market' 72 : the outcome of the behaviour of numerous individuals, each
seeking to achieve its own objectives, and entering into contractual relation-
ship with others in order to do so.
This understanding of the firm effectively spirits it out of existence. A key
question that had faced economists engaged in theorising the nature of the
firm, the question of scale of the firm-what factors limit the size of the
firm relative to the market in which it operates-also becomes irrelevant.
In Jensen and Meckling's theory of the firm, it does not make sense to try
to distinguish things which are 'inside' the firm and things that are
'outside' the firm. There is 'in a very real sense, only a multitude of
complex relationships (ie contracts).' 73 Concerns about 'giant corporations'
disappear if the firm is merely another way to describe contractual relations
between individuals, and if there is no 'inside' or 'outside' to the firm. Talk of
corporate power is, as Alchian and Demsetz insisted, 'delusional': 'The firm
[…] has no power of fiat, no authority, no disciplinary action any different in
the slightest degree from ordinary market contracting between any two
people'. 74 The contracts around which the firm is constituted are merely
the product of market forces to which all contracting parties both 'within'
and 'outside' the firm are subject to.
Jensen and Meckling's theory of the firm is embraced by corporate
lawyers. Already in the early 1960s Henry Manne, who can claim to be the
founder of law and economics, bemoaned the 'lack of a systematic, integrated
economic analysis of the modern corporation' and the attempt to apply
moral or political, rather than economic, standards to the corporation. 75
In a latter article Manne welcomed the 'more realistic appraisal of the dispa-
rate interests in large corporations' which could counter the 'anachronistic
view of the corporation as an aggregate which could be viewed and analysed
as a single entity'. 76
Frank Easterbrook and Daniel Fischel sought to 'explain the structure of
corporate law' by using the Jensen and Meckling's nexus of contracts theory
as 'the engine that drives [corporate law]. 77 They reiterate that 'the

What is real is the market, that is to say 'economic interactions among people
dealing as strangers and seeking personal advantage'. Within that market,
some people may opt to 'band together' for longer periods of time, where
they consider that this is to their individual advantage, and in this way
firms arise. 78 Corporations are a subset of firms characterised by a specific
financing device. 79
The nexus of contracts analogy 'focuses the attention on the voluntary and
adaptive nature' of the 'corporation'. 80 Firms arise out of a series of voluntary
choices that individual market actors make in response to market signals.
The way in which the firm is structured, and what contractual arrangements
regulate the relationship between the different individuals within the firm-
the firm's governance structure-are shaped by market forces as well.
According to Easterbrook and Fischel, 'self-interested … managers are
driven to find the devices most likely to maximise net profit [for the inves-
tors]'. The arrangements which are found, through the operation of the
market, to be optimal for the firms and the investors are also, necessarily,
optimal for society. 81
Corporate law, on Easterbrook and Fischel's view, is merely 'a set of terms
available off-the-rack so that participants in corporate ventures can save the
cost of contracting'. 82 This understanding of the corporation rejects the
claim advanced by Haansman et al, discussed above 83 , that individuals
would be unable to secure entity shielding through contract. As Jensen
and Meckling emphasise in a later article, 'the corporation requires for its
existence only freedom of contract'. 84
The legal provisions stipulating how the corporation is to be governed
reflect the terms that the different parties 'would have bargained for had
they anticipated the problems and been able to transact costlessly in
advance'. 85 On this view, rather than the corporation being a creature of
law, as it is often stated, law is a creature of the corporation. Or rather,
given that the corporation is a mere fiction, law is a creature of the inter-
action of individual market actors seeking to maximise their own prefer-
ences. The corporate code is an 'enabling statute', and rather than
reflecting political decisions about how corporations should be governed,

it merely fills-in the blanks in the open-ended contractual provisions which
the parties agree between themselves. Therefore, according to Easterbrook
and Fischel 'there is no reason why [the law] should be used to impose a
term that defeats actual bargains or reduces the venturers' joint wealth'. 86
Even legislators become market actors in this view. The role of state law is
seen as an element in the private ordering of contractual relationships, which
provides the parties with 'jurisdictional choice in the market for corporate
charters'. 87 States 'fish for successful combinations' of corporate law pro-
visions. 88 States know that managers will search for the legal rules that will
allow them to maximise investors welfare, so there will be competitive
pressure for states to legislate corporate codes that are attractive to
investors. 89
Fiduciary rules in corporate law appear to be inconsistent with the con-
tractual approach. The general rule is that directors and other officers of the
company have a duty of care and loyalty towards the company. 90 If there is
no such thing as a company, as an entity towards which an individual may
exercise loyalty or care, this requirement would seem to break down. The
contractarians' response is that such 'duties' should be seen a part of con-
tractual protection against managerial mismanagement which has been
implicitly negotiated for by the parties to the corporate contractual relation-
ships. 91 That still leaves the question of to whom such 'duties' are owed.
The corporation as an entity to whom the duty is owed is replaced by an
amorphous notion of 'corporate interest'. 92 For Easterbrook and Fischel
the duties of loyalty and care 'attach to the residual claim'. 93 This may
seem nonsensical-to owe a duty to a column in a ledger. Fama and
Jensen justify the centrality of the residual claim in the nexus of contractual
relations by attempting to show that it is those (ie, the shareholders) who
contract for the residual claim, which they define as 'the difference
between stochastic inflows of resources and promised payment' who bear

the residual risk. 94 As such, it is they-the shareholders-who have most at
stake in the decisions of those running the company. 95
The understanding of the corporation as a nexus of contracts-also call
the contractarian theory-has come to dominate academic thinking about
the corporation 96 to such an extent that it may appear to be an expression
of the objective reality of the corporate form. However, if we approach the
nexus of contract theory as a story-a story designed to address worries
about corporate power, we can see that it neutralises such worries by
making it appear that corporations do not exist. According to this story,
all that exists are individuals, seeking to further their own interests, entering
into contractual relationships with others in order to do so. The companies
that come into being as a result of these arrangements are not contingent and
artificial-they are necessary and natural. Corporate laws are not the product
of political decisions, they are the outcome of 'natural' selection-of market
forces operating on the legislators. Those laws that corporations find most
attractive are therefore objectively the best. They are necessarily the best
possible laws.
4. The entrepreneur story
The myth of the entrepreneur has been a central pillar of free market ideol-
ogy from its earliest days. The term was probably coined by Jean-Baptiste
Say, 97 who developed what Boutillier and Uzundis describe as the 'heroic'
notion of the entrepreneur. 98 This superior kind of person, who exercises
'Judgment, perseverance, and a knowledge of the world, as well as of
business' 99 played a key role in the nineteenth century idea of how
markets function because 'he directs the business of production, and is the
centre of many bearings and relations'. 100 This heroic entrepreneur must
be prepared to stake his own fortune and reputation on his 'judgment,

perseverance and knowledge of the world'. 101 The entrepreneur, on this
understanding, is the person who sets the enterprise in motion, plans and
organises production, and who puts up his own (or borrowed) capital, and
who takes all contingent risks. 102 Because of this, it is the entrepreneur
who should receive all profits from the enterprise.
Say was writing at the start of the nineteenth century. He practiced what
he preached, having himself invested his money, and that of his business
partner, in a cotton mill, which he had had built and which he managed
himself. At that time, the modern company did not exist. Over the next
hundred years, the modern company would evolve to become 'the principal
factor in economic organization'. 103 This is a development that Say could
hardly have predicted, 104 and which makes untenable this understanding
of the 'heroic' entrepreneur that risks his own capital by setting in motion
an enterprise which he directs and controls. The occupation of 'adventurer'
or entrepreneur, as described and theorised by Say, no longer seems relevant
in this new world. As Berle and Means describe, the modern company
entails:
[an] aggregation in which tens and even hundreds of thousands of workers and
property worth hundreds of millions of dollars, belonging to tens or even hun-
dreds of thousands of individuals, are combined through the corporate mech-
anism into a single producing organization under unified control and
management. 105
Under this regime, the owners of the capital are no longer those who control
the company. The control of the company is in the hands of hired managers,
and the ownership is in the hand of countless individuals who have little
ability or desire to oversee the running of the company. 106 Berle and
Means contend that the modern company, by dissolving the 'atom of own-
ership' comprised of beneficial ownership and control, 'destroys the very
foundations of the economic order [based on private enterprise]'. A
central foundation of this economic order is the idea that 'the individual is
protected in the right both to use his own property as he sees fit and to

104 Berle and Means note that, at the time they were writing (1933) 'men still living can recall a time
when the present situation was hardly dreamed of'. The historical veracity of Berle and Means analy-
sis has been questioned (Eric Hilt, 'The "Berle and Means Corporation' in an Historical Perspective'
(2019) 42 Seattle University Law Review 417). Nonetheless, it is clear that the prevalence and scale
of business companies (as well as the nature of their legal form) were profoundly transformed
over the course of the Nineteenth Century and early Twentieth Century, in ways that were not fore-
seen by Say and his contemporaries.

106 As Berle and Means put it 'a large body of security holders has been created who exercise virtually no
control over the wealth which they or their predecessors in interest have contributed to the enter-

text.body:
receive the full fruits of its use'. 107 This will produce appropriate incentives
which will guarantee an efficient economic order. 108 With the rise of modern
corporations, this foundational element of the economic order is destroyed,
and with it the ideal of the heroic entrepreneur who puts up his or her own
capital and runs the company so as to profit from it.
Furthermore, as discussed above, Bearle and Means go on to argue that,
because the modern corporation has become a social institution, rather
than a private one, it must be run as such, in order to serve the interests
of all society. 109
We have seen in the previous section that, in response to the demand that
the corporation be subject to public control, so as to ensure that they com-
plied with demands of corporate social responsibility and acted in the benefit
of all, Jensen and Meckling, together with others, developed the 'nexus of
contracts' story, where the company disappears. However, in this story,
the entrepreneur also disappears. There is no individual who sets the enter-
prise in motion, or who plans and directs the action of the enterprise,
because there is no enterprise. Individuals are contracting with each other
to further their individual interests in the market. 110 The story of the
nexus of contracts appears to have no place for the entrepreneur.
However, in a book published in the same year as Berle and Means's opus,
Frank Knight gave us a different story. 111
Knight's insight is that the world we live in is 'a world of change […] and a
world of uncertainty'. 112 The import of this insight is that not all actors in the
market are equal. Some have a specific role in anticipating demand in the
face of incomplete knowledge and to exercise judgment so as to control pro-
duction in order meet and even create demand. The primary phase of econ-
omic organisation is, on this view, the production of goods for a market. 113
In the face of uncertainty as to what goods will be in demand in the market, a
new figure gains centre stage-the entrepreneur. It is the entrepreneur's
hands that the specialisation of 'uncertainty bearing' is placed. 114 This
special social class of men [sic] 'direct economic activity; they are, in the
text.note:
110 In the 'nexus of contracts' story 'the firm has no center and the old fashioned term and concept has
no function to play' (Charles O'Kelley, 'Coase, Knight, and the Nexus-of-Contracts Theory of the Firm'
(2012) 35 Seattle University Law Review 1247, 1249). O'Kelley lamented that 'in their zeal to reestablish
individualism and contractarian analysis [the proponents of the Nexus of Contracts theory] also threw
out the "classic entrepreneur"'. Charles O'Kelley, 'The Entrepreneur and the Theory of the Modern
Corporation' (2006) 31 Journal of Corporate Law 753.
111 Frank Knight, Risk, Uncertainty and Profit (Houghton Mifflin co, 1933).
text.body:
strict sense, the producers' 115 because they are the ones who, in the presence
of uncertainty, 'decide […] what to do and how to do it'. 116
Knight therefore attributes to entrepreneurs the two inseparable elements
of responsibility and control. 117 In this Knight is in agreement with Say. 118
How can this be reconciled with the modern company where, as Berle and
Means point out 119 , ownership is separated from control? Knight begins
by accepting that, in a modern company concentrated control is combined
with diffused ownership. 120 This may give the impression that there is a 'sep-
aration of the functions of making decisions and taking the "risk" in the error
in decisions'. 121 However, this separation is illusory:
When control is accurately defined and located, the functions of making
decisions and assuming the responsibility for their correctness will be found
to be one and indivisible. 122
In a company, the workers perform the tasks assigned to them. They need to
exercise a degree of judgment in how to perform those tasks, but the respon-
sibility for his or her work is of the supervisor who choses that worker and
instructs that worker. The supervisor is in turn appointed by, and under the
supervision of the manager, and 'on up the scale the same relations hold
good until we come to the supreme head of the business' 123 (eg the CEO).
But even the work of this 'supreme head' is 'a routine tasks of exercising
his best judgment' 124 According to Knight, the real responsibility is not on
the one who decides 'on the concrete ordering of policy, but ordering an
orderer as a "labourer" to order it'. 125 The crucial decision, and the exercise
of responsible control, fall on the owners of the productive services used in
the business. In this way, entrepreneurship is distributed and divided in a
typical modern business organisation among the shareholders who own
the company. 126
In his theory, Knight replaces the entrepreneur as the person who both
owns the company and who directs and controls it, with a diffuse and
divided 'entrepreneurship' that is assigned to shareholders. They have

Knight's work did not have a significant impact at the time. Berle and Means
represented the consensus view among economists and corporate lawyers.
This continued well into the post war years, which scholars like Chandler
-'secret of economic success lay not in individualism and entrepreneurship,
but in management coordination and the cooperation of employees'. 130 Even
Schumpeter, who developed an influential theory of the role of the entrepre-
neur in a capitalist society was pessimistic about the place of such a person
within advanced capitalist economies. Schumpeter foresaw the decline of
capitalism with the rise of socialised production within large bureaucratic
firms. Within such firms 'Bureau and committee work tends to replace indi-
vidual action' and the 'flash of genius' of entrepreneurial spirit becomes
redundant. 131
However, as Plehwe shows, a group of economists associated with the
Mount Pelerin Society 'rebutted, revived and revised Schumpeter's theory
of the entrepreneur from the 1950s to the 80s'. 132 Scholars such as von
Mises and Hayek used the figure of the entrepreneur to postulate 'universal
characteristics of economic humankind'. 133 They grounded the 'Austrian'
school of economic theory, which provides us with an understanding of
the market where the 'entrepreneur' could exist despite the existence of
the firm. In fact, whereas Knight sought to locate the entrepreneur within
the organisational structure of the firm, the Austrians never really 'shown
much interest in a theory of the firm'. 134 Nonetheless, their theory of entre-
preneurship has profound implications for how the company is understood
within economic processes.

According to Kirzner, the features which distinguishes the Austrian tra-
dition from what he describes as 'mainstream classic economic theory' are:
(a) market equilibrium is a dynamic process rather than a state and (b)
the force which drives this dynamic process is entrepreneurial discovery.
In mainstream economic theory, market actors are theorised as successful
maximising agents-they have complete information and are able to
achieve market equilibrium. In such a model of the market, there is no
role for the entrepreneur because there is no room for uncertainty, and
as we have seen from Knight, the entrepreneur is the 'uncertainty
bearing' agent in the market. The Austrians propose a dynamic model of
the market, where:
entrepreneurial discovery … gradually but systematically push[es] back the
boundaries of sheer ignorance … increasing mutual awareness among
market participants and thus, in turn, driving prices, output and input quan-
tities and qualities towards the values consistent with equilibrium 135
In this model, entrepreneurs make decisions in the face of uncertainty. They
may be mistaken, but any mistakes 'tend to be corrected … through the
responsiveness of alert, imaginative entrepreneurs to the opportunities
revealed as a result of [these mistakes]'. 136 So while the Austrian tradition
does not claim that entrepreneurial discovery will lead to complete mutual
awareness and thereby market equilibrium, it does claim that entrepreneurial
discovery does result in a 'tendency towards' mutual awareness and market
equilibrium.
In contrast to the 'mainstream classical approach' that locates those spon-
taneous forces in the minds of individuals who are all seeking to maximise
their own individual preferences in a system of perfect competition, the Aus-
trian approach locates the driving force in 'acts of entrepreneurial
discovery' 137
5. Rights of companies-reinforcing and justifying the stories
The previous two sections show how the story of the nexus of contracts and
the story of the entrepreneur can be seen as two different narratives which
counter concerns about corporate power and demands for greater political
control over corporations. In the following section I will argue that these
stories about companies are accompanied by two corresponding stories
about rights, which reinforce and legitimate the stories about companies. I
will present the caselaw of the US Supreme Court and of the Court of

the nexus of contract and the entrepreneur story.
5.1. The constitutional rights of companies in the US Supreme Court
As set out above, the nexus of contracts story denies the existence of the cor-
poration as an entity. As such there are no corporations to exercise power or
authority, or to shoulder responsibilities. It must therefore follow that there
can be no question of the company itself enjoying any rights. Any rights that
the law may afford the corporation must necessarily be the rights of the indi-
viduals who contract through the corporation. As Mekling and Jensen put it,
in a later article, regulatory controls on corporations in order to achieve
public benefits, such as protection from discrimination or environmental
protection, entail a deprivation of the property rights, not of the company,
but of shareholders and other 'owners' of the corporation, in order to trans-
fer wealth 'to […] other groups -women, blacks, consumers of a clean
environment, etc'. 138 Similarity, laws of co-determination in Europe are pre-
sented as an interference, not with the freedom of the company, but with the
contractual rights of directors and shareholders and managers'. 139 Under this
view 'all rights are […] human rights; there can be no other kind' because
only individuals human beings exist as subjects of rights. 140
For over 200 years the Supreme Court has accepted that corporations
could enjoy the protection of federal constitutional rights. 141 However, the
approach to the nature of the corporation as the bearer of those rights
appears remarkably vague. In Bank of the United States v Deveaux, Chief
Justice Marshall, giving the opinion of the majority, affirmed that, on a ques-
tion of jurisdiction, the Court could look behind the corporate entity to 'the
character of the individuals who compose the corporation'. Because those
individuals were US citizens, the corporation had standing, even if 'that
invisible, intangible, and artificial being, that mere legal entity, a corporation
aggregate, [was] certainly not a citizen'. Nonetheless, the same Chief Justice
would, ten years later, describe the corporation as an entity that can 'manage
its own affairs, […] hold property' and realise the purposes for which it was
created. 142
This ambiguity as to the nature of the corporation reappeared in the
notorious case of Citizen's United. 143 The case concerned a challenge by a

from engaging in certain kind of political speech within 30 days of an elec-

were unique kinds of legal entities that enjoyed a number of state-conferred
privileges which allowed it to exert undue influence in the political
process. 144 In Citizens United the court reversed its decision, on the
grounds that it was impermissible for the government to ban speech
'simply because the speaker is an association that has taken on the corporate
form'. Adam Winkler asserts that, in Citizens United the Supreme Court pro-
tected the rights of corporations 'because corporations are comprised of
people, and those people have rights that ought to be respected regardless
of the use of the corporate form'. 145 Not all commentators share this
reading of the case. David Rosenberg considers that the majority opinion
'plainly rests on protecting the constitutional rights of corporate decision
makers' rather than of the shareholders. 146 Whilst I do not agree with Rosen-
berg; and Scalia's concurring opinion in Citizens United is even more explicit
that the First Amendment protects 'incorporated associations of individ-
uals', 147 the case does show considerable ambiguity as to whose rights are
protected and on what grounds.
In the subsequent case of Hobby Lobby, the Supreme Court was more
explicit as to the grounds for protecting the constitutional rights of the cor-
poration. As Chief Justice Alito put it in his opinion for the majority 'when
rights, whether constitutional or statutory, are extended to corporations, the
purpose is to protect the rights of [the people associated with the corpor-
ation]'. Oliver points out, in his contribution to this special issue, that the
Supreme Court does not account for the fact that a corporation is 'a legal
entity in its own right' but treats it instead as a group of individuals. As
Winkler puts it, in Hobby Lobby the Court 'abandons the core tenet of cor-
porate personhood: that a corporation is an independent legal entity with
rights and duties wholly separate and apart from those of its members'. 148
This understanding of the basis of corporate rights was reiterated in 303
Creative. 149 The case concerned a Colorado state law that prohibited 'public
facing businesses' from denying 'the full and equal enjoyment' of its goods
and services to any customer based inter alia sexual orientation. 303 Creative

design services to the public. In holding that 303 Creative could deny services
to gay customers, Chief Justice Gorsuch framed the case as a restriction on
the religious freedom of Ms Smith, the sole member and employee of the
company. There was no mention of 303 Creative as the corporate petition,
beyond the statement that 'speakers [do not] shed their First Amendment
protections by employing the corporate form to disseminate their speech'.
As this author put it in an earlier comment on this case 'this seems to
present the company as merely a garb which individuals can put on or
remove at their choosing'. 150 Oliver counters that 'To all intents and pur-
poses, when acting in her professional capacity, Ms Smith was indistinguish-
able from 303 Creative'. This, however, ignores longstanding caselaw, going
back to Salomon v Salomon & Co, which insists that 'the company is at law a
different person altogether from [its] subscribers'. 151 This is the case even in
respect of a sole shareholder of a closely held corporation. 152 As Macey and
Strine point out, in a range of other areas of law, such as tax law, or criminal
or civil liability, the Supreme Court has consistently treated corporations as
distinct entities from its shareholders. 153
5.2. Protecting entrepreneurial processes in the Court of Justice of
the EU
In contrast to the nexus of contracts story, in the entrepreneur story, the
rights of the individuals who make up the corporation are not so central.
After all, most of the 'great mass of the population' who make up the corpor-
ation, from employees to managers, are merely instruments by which entre-
preneurial discovery can be brought about. Government regulation of
corporations in not necessarily objectionable on the grounds that it interferes
with the rights of market participants, but rather because:
government regulation of market activity is likely to obstruct and frustrate the
spontaneous, corrective forces of entrepreneurial adjustment. 154
It is entrepreneurial processes which, by creating new markets and finding
new opportunities, drive economic development in advanced economies. 155

Therefore, the rights of companies are valuable because, and to the extent
that, such rights protect or promote these entrepreneurial processes.
This instrumental understanding of fundamental rights chimes well with
the Court of Justice's approach to fundamental rights adjudication. As the
Court itself stated:
The reason for pursuing [the objective of protecting fundamental rights in EU
law] is the need to avoid a situation in which the level of protection of funda-
mental rights varies according to the national law involved in such a way as to
undermine the unity, primacy and effectiveness of EU law 156
The EU is a purposive polity, 157 and as such only has the competence to do
that which is necessary to achieve the objectives set out in the Treaties. 158
This purposive nature of the EU remains relevant also when interpreting
and applying EU fundamental rights, and the protection of such rights
'must be ensured within the framework of the structure and objectives of
the [EU]'. 159
The central objective of the EU has been, and remains, the internal market
project. 160 As Weatherill explains, the 'EU's commitment made by Article
3(3) TEU to the establishment of an internal market carries constitutional
significance' because this commitment delineates and legitimates the exercise
of EU competence. 161 The 'unity, primacy and effectiveness' of EU law to
which the CJEU refers in the Siragusa quote above are the necessary con-
ditions of this internal market-it is because the EU has the objective of
creating an internal market that creates the requirement for EU law to be
uniform across the member states, to enjoy primacy over national laws
that may impede free movement, and to be effectively implemented in the
member states legal order. National fundamental rights may undermine
this unity, primacy and effectiveness, so EU fundamental rights must be
applied autonomously in a way that ensures that this does not happen. 162
As Isiksel puts it:
human rights norms were introduced into the market-oriented legal system of
the EC as a judicially affixed band-aid, intended to preserve its unity and
autonomy against the threat of defection by national courts. 163

This instrumentality of EU fundamental rights, and their contingency on the
EU internal market objectives, remains to this day. As Augenstein insists:
[EU) fundamental rights' contingency on, and subordination to, fundamental
[market] freedoms … is rooted in the systemic conditions for an autonomous
interpretation of fundamental rights in a supra-national European polity
whose fundamental boundary is the internal market. 164
In light of the internal market objective, 165 corporations have been granted
extensive economic freedoms, 166 and the fundamental rights of other
market actors have been subordinated to these economic freedoms. 167
However, in a recent line of cases, beginning with Alemo Herron, 168 the
Court of Justice has protected the rights of corporations, even in situations
where free movement, and the internal market objective, did not appear to
be at stake. As Bartl and Leone point out 'unlike in Laval and related
cases, the limitation of workers' rights [in Alemo Herron] is not offered up
on the altar of fundamental freedoms but fundamental rights'. 169
This case involved a company that was required to comply with national
legislation which protected the rights of workers in cases where the company
they worked for was taken over by another company. The Court held that
this legislation violated the company's right to conduct business under
Article 16 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU. While this
right was originally seen as a 'weak right' 170 that only protected the rights
of corporations to conduct business to the extent that national and EU law
permitted, it has, as this author argues, 171 been transformed in the Court's
caselaw into a general rule that protects the right of corporations 'to
conduct their business as they see fit.' 172 In subsequent cases it has been
relied on by companies to challenge laws protecting workers from

There has been no noticeable attempt on the part of the Court to explain
why the right of corporations to be free from regulatory control should be
protected. The current President of the Court has written (extrajudicially)
of the need to protect the 'private autonomy' of market actors. 175 The Fun-
damental Rights Agency states that 'the essence of the freedom to conduct a
business is to enable individual aspirations and expression to flourish'. 176
This seems to tie the value of the right to conduct business to the what
Dan-Cohen calls 'the autonomy paradigm', which ascribes intrinsic value
to the protection of the autonomy of individuals. However, as Dan-Cohen
notes, this paradigm is not a good fit for the rights of corporations,
because a corporation is an intelligent machine, and there is no intrinsic
value in protecting its autonomy. 177
A more plausible explanation is provided by Nils Wahl, currently a Judge
at the Court of Justice. Writing extra-judicially, Wahl states that:
the freedom to conduct a business forms part of the EU's economic consti-
tution according to which Member States have undertaken to commit to a
specific form of political economy. 178
In this framing, the rights of corporations are justified not by reference to the
nature of the corporate entity, but by the need to uphold a certain kind of
'political economy', one where 'the state must, in essence, refrain from regu-
lation'. 179 The justification for this imperative on the state to regulate corpor-
ations is not made clear. The Fundamental Rights Agency's Report cited
above went on to assert that 'the essence of the freedom to conduct a business
is […] to promote entrepreneurship and innovation, which in turn is indis-
pensable for sustainable social and economic development'. 180 This is echoed
by Usai, who claims that protecting the freedom to conduct business:
is not designed to protect the subjective positions of any market players but
rather it is conceived as a tool for protecting the benefits directly or indirectly
deriving from a single, free, and competitive market. 181

The right of corporations to conduct business in the EU is framed as an instru-
ment in the construction of a certain kind of market, and an instrument to facili-
tate processes within which entrepreneurial discovery can take place.
6. Conclusion
In this article I presented two stories which respond to, and counter, concerns
about corporate power. These stories shape our world. As Chen and Hansen
argue, the knowledge structures which constitute our 'internal situation' and
which guide are behaviour are made up of the 'categories, schemas and
scripts through which we interpret and respond to the world around us'. 182
Both these stories shift the focus away from the corporation as an entity
that acts in the world, that exercises power and that has its own interests
and objectives. I have shown that the corporation as a form of technology
was developed over hundreds of years, as the outcome of contingent and
contested political decisions. The effect of these narratives is to hide this
technology-to hide the machine. In the nexus of contracts story the corpor-
ation is effectively spirited out of existence, and all that is left are individual
human beings, autonomously contracting with each other in the market. In
the entrepreneur story, corporations, to the extent that they are considered,
are presented as part of processes within which individual entrepreneurs can
engage in acts of entrepreneurial discovery, anticipating risk, dealing with
uncertainty and identifying opportunities for profit. These stories work as
shields, deflecting calls for greater corporate accountability, or demands
for corporate social responsibility.
Linked to these stories about companies, I identified two stories about
rights that seem to fit the stories about corporations. The rights stories
work as swords, justifying and legitimating challenges to regulations con-
straining the exercise of power by corporations. They make it possible for
corporations to argue that regulations that were enacted in order to
protect rights of vulnerable human beings-workers, consumers, citizens-
are instead breaches of the fundamental rights those corporations.
